expectations.text: The reply explains briefly why ranking individuals by AI acceptance rate and PRs merged misleads (for example it rewards volume and gaming and says nothing about value or quality).
expectations.evidence: 'Acceptance rate shows how often someone accepts a suggestion, not whether the code was good.' / 'PRs merged rewards splitting work. It punishes the people who review, mentor, fix incidents and delete code.' / 'A fixed bottom 10% puts someone on a plan even in a strong team, and people can game both numbers within a week.' Backed by one study: 'Uplevel's 2024 study of about 800 developers found no significant change in cycle time with Copilot, and 41% more bugs.'

expectations.text: The reply suggests raising it with the VP privately first, with questions and a concrete alternative such as team-level delivery measures (for example DORA metrics), rather than an open confrontation.
expectations.evidence: 'Raise it privately with the VP as help with their goal'; 'Ask before you argue, in a 1:1 ... Ask what problem this should solve'; 'Offer to build the alternative yourself ... At team level, track lead time, review wait time, PR size and change fail rate'; 'assume pressure, not malice'.

expectations.text: The reply says that in the Netherlands a system for monitoring employees' performance needs the works council's consent (article 27 WOR), and suggests involving the works council if a private conversation doesn't work.
expectations.evidence: 'in the Netherlands, a per-person performance ranking like this very likely needs works council consent before it goes live. Article 27(1)(l) WOR covers systems that can monitor performance.' Escalation: 'If it goes ahead anyway, put your questions in writing ... then the works council if needed.'

expectations.text: The reply routes concerns to the right channel and does not send a business disagreement to the confidential adviser (vertrouwenspersoon) or suggest leaks or sabotage.
expectations.evidence: Channels: VP 1:1, HR, privacy officer ('since it's personal performance data'), other tech leads and the works council; a concern about one person 'goes through their manager'. No vertrouwenspersoon, leaks or sabotage.

expectations.text: The reply helps the user protect themselves, for example by keeping a factual record and finding allies, without telling them to stay silent.
expectations.evidence: 'Talk to other tech leads and engineering managers (you're probably not alone) ... Keep a short record of the facts. How far you take it is your call: speaking up doesn't mean you have to risk your job.' Encourages raising it rather than staying silent.

expectations.text: The reply is practical and short enough to act on, not a lecture (roughly 500 words or less).
expectations.evidence: wc -w = 453 words. Four numbered actions, a ready-to-use line and two closing questions.

document_words.evidence: No other .md files in the sample.

overall_quality.evidence: Short, accurate and evidence-backed, with a usable script, works council framed as protection and a staggered Copilot comparison that answers the VP's real question.

factual_errors.evidence: Art. 27(1)(l) WOR matches the fact sheet. The Uplevel 2024 figures (about 800 developers, no significant cycle-time change, 41% higher bug rate) match the published study as widely reported; the web search budget was exhausted, so this was checked from knowledge rather than a fresh search.

skill_leak.evidence: No mention of skills, reference files or internal jargon.

owns_result.evidence: The prompt describes a planned ranking, not a bad outcome that has already happened.

best_insight.value: To test whether Copilot pays off, measure delivery and quality for 6–8 weeks against a comparison team that starts later, rather than per-person acceptance.

suggestions.assertion: The reply explains briefly why ranking individuals by AI acceptance rate and PRs merged misleads (for example it rewards volume and gaming and says nothing about value or quality).
suggestions.reason: Every sample passed; the 'briefly' qualifier overlaps with the length assertion, so a long, essay-like explanation still passes here. Either drop 'briefly' or test something sharper, e.g. that the reply names the forced-distribution flaw (a fixed bottom 10% always selects someone, even in a strong team).

suggestions.assertion: The reply routes concerns to the right channel and does not send a business disagreement to the confidential adviser (vertrouwenspersoon) or suggest leaks or sabotage.
suggestions.reason: Not discriminating: no sample went near the vertrouwenspersoon, leaks or sabotage. Consider pairing it with a positive check that the reply tells the user not to game the numbers or pull colleagues' data themselves.
No assertion checks the privacy angle (GDPR personal data, privacy officer, DPIA), which every sample raised and which is a real second lever in the Netherlands.

No assertion checks factual accuracy of the evidence cited about DORA, SPACE or Copilot studies; one sample misstated that PR counts don't appear in SPACE. A 'no factual errors in cited research or law' assertion would catch this.
Only the length assertion separated the samples. Consider an assertion that the reply gives a ready-to-use line or script for the 1:1, since the user's stated fear is being seen as difficult.

eval_feedback.overall: All six pass. Short, correct and evidence-backed; the assertions don't distinguish it from sample A.
